When assessing the vaginal dose during image-guided brachytherapy for cervical cancer, healthcare providers can primarily rely on dose-point evaluation. This method involves evaluating doses at specific points where the radiation source is closest to the target area within the cervix. These points are typically defined as points in the PIBS (Point Intra-Biopsy Specimen) or PIBS +2 locations.

During image-guided brachytherapy, these dose-point evaluations take place during the treatment process using imaging modalities such as digital radiography or ultrasound guidance. The doses evaluated at these specific points are compared to the planned target volume in terms of both conformity and homogeneity to ensure that the radiation dose is accurately delivered to the tumor while minimizing exposure to surrounding healthy tissues.

The use of dose-point evaluation allows for a detailed assessment of the dosimetric accuracy of the treatment plan, which is crucial for evaluating the effectiveness of brachytherapy in treating cervical cancer. If doses evaluated at PIBS points are not impacted by intrafractional movements, it means that any movement within the breast tissue during the course of the treatment will not alter the delivered dose to the target.

Furthermore, studies such as the one mentioned in Prompt 3 (Vaginal dose assessment in image-guided brachytherapy for cervical cancer: Can we really rely on dose-point evaluation) support the reliability of this method. These preliminary results suggest that doses evaluated at PIBS and PIBS +2 dose points allow distinguishing the plans of patients with vaginal infiltration, indicating their feasibility.

In summary, healthcare providers can rely on dose-point evaluation to assess the vaginal dose during image-guided brachytherapy for cervical cancer as it accurately reflects the delivered radiation dose within the target volume while considering any intrafractional movements.
